learning_goal: Explain why the straight heart tube must bend, describe the normal D-loop as a set of three movements, say where each of the five segments finishes after looping and why that arrangement is what septation needs, and use left-right patterning to account for L-loop, dextrocardia and the heterotaxy syndromes.

views.title: Why a straight tube cannot stay straight
views.narration: By day twenty-three the heart tube is tied at both ends — arteries above, veins below — and it is elongating faster than the pericardial cavity around it. Cells added at both poles from the secondary heart field keep lengthening it. A tube that is growing, held at both ends and running out of room can only do one thing, and it bends. Looping is mechanics before it is genetics; the genes decide which way, not whether.

views.title: The dorsal mesocardium has already broken down
views.narration: The middle of the dorsal mesocardium has already given way, so the tube hangs free between its two fixed ends. That is what makes bending possible at all. The gap it leaves behind is the transverse pericardial sinus, which is why in the adult you can pass a finger behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk and in front of the atria.

views.title: Movement one — the bulbus swings ventrally, caudally and to the RIGHT
views.narration: The first movement is the one that names the loop. The bulbus cordis, the cranial half of the tube, swings forwards, downwards and to the right. That is the D-loop, D for dextro, and it is the normal direction in every healthy human heart. Say it as one sentence you can repeat under exam pressure: the bulbus goes ventral, caudal and right.

views.title: Movement two — the ventricle swings dorsally and to the LEFT
views.narration: The second movement is the mirror of the first. The primitive ventricle moves backwards and to the left. Bulbus to the right, ventricle to the left, and the two now sit side by side rather than one behind the other. The groove between them outside is the bulboventricular sulcus, and the opening between them inside is the primary interventricular foramen — the hole the muscular septum will later grow up towards.

views.title: Movement three — the atria climb up behind
views.narration: The third movement carries the atrium and the sinus venosus backwards and upwards, so the inflow end comes to lie behind and above the ventricles instead of below them. This is the movement that produces the adult arrangement: atria posterior and superior, ventricles anterior and inferior, and the great vessels rising between the two atria in front. Every relation you learn in the adult mediastinum was set here.

views.title: What the loop leaves you with
views.narration: By about day twenty-eight the tube has become an S. The two future ventricles lie side by side, the two future atria lie side by side behind and above them, the atrioventricular canal joins the atrial half to the ventricular half, and the outflow tract runs up in the midline between the atria. Nothing has been divided yet — this is one continuous lumen. But the pieces are now in the right places relative to each other.

views.title: Looping is the setup for septation
views.narration: Understand looping as the step that brings each part alongside the part it must be joined to. The septa built next are all short walls between structures that looping has already parked next to one another. That is why a looping or alignment error shows up later as a connection fault rather than a hole: the great arteries coming off the wrong ventricle, or both off the right. If the pieces are put in the wrong place, no amount of correct wall-building fixes it.

views.title: L-loop — the tube turns the wrong way
views.narration: If the tube loops to the left instead of the right, the ventricles end up inverted — the morphological right ventricle on the left and the left ventricle on the right. When the great arteries are also transposed, the two errors cancel each other for flow and the child is pink: congenitally corrected transposition. Do not read 'corrected' as 'normal'. The right ventricle is pumping to the body for a lifetime, and it fails eventually, with conduction tissue that is abnormally placed and prone to block.

views.title: Dextrocardia — and the difference from dextroposition
views.narration: Dextrocardia means the heart is built pointing to the right; dextroposition means a normal heart has been pushed to the right by something else, such as a right lung agenesis or a left tension pneumothorax. The distinction is the first thing to make on the film. When dextrocardia comes with full situs inversus the internal relations are a clean mirror image and the heart is usually otherwise normal. Isolated dextrocardia, with the abdominal organs in the usual place, carries a high rate of associated defects. About a quarter of situs inversus cases are Kartagener syndrome, where immotile cilia give bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis and infertility alongside the mirrored anatomy — one ciliary defect, four findings.

Dextrocardia is shown using the L-loop build. REVIEW 2026-09-10: that is not honest enough to stand as written. Mirror-image dextrocardia with situs inversus is L-looped, but DEXTROVERSION — isolated dextrocardia with the abdominal organs in the usual place, which is the case this view's own narration calls out as carrying a high rate of associated defects — is a D-looped heart rotated into the right chest. Showing only the mirrored loop teaches L-loop = dextrocardia. Dextrocardia is also a claim about position and apex direction within the thorax, and this model has no body midline and no chest, so the picture cannot make that claim at all: nothing in the frame says right or left. Neither dextroposition nor dextroversion is shown. Recorded as a defect awaiting the build task, not as an accepted limitation.
Septation is named as the consequence of looping but not built; it is its own scene (septation-of-heart).

The pericardial cavity IS built by the model (key 'pericardium') but is not used by this scene. Two reasons, both of which are defects in the model rather than choices: it is drawn at opacity 0.022, which is invisible, and it is sized from the bounding box of the heart at that same t, so it grows with the tube. View 1's narration says the tube is elongating faster than the cavity around it; a cavity scaled to the tube can never show that. Declared here so the key is accounted for, not endorsed.

deferred_beats.title: What decides right rather than left
deferred_beats.narration: The direction of the loop is decided before the loop happens. Motile cilia at the primitive node sweep fluid to the left, that leftward flow switches on Nodal and then Pitx2 in the left lateral plate mesoderm, and the two sides of the embryo stop being equivalent. The heart tube reads that asymmetry and turns to the right. So laterality is a week-three event with a week-four consequence, and a cilia defect explains a heart defect.
deferred_beats.why_not_a_view: The mechanism is at the PRIMITIVE NODE, days before the loop and in a different structure: motile cilia sweeping fluid leftward, Nodal, then Pitx2. A model of the heart tube cannot show any of it.
deferred_beats.belongs_in: embryology__week-3-gastrulation__primitive-streak — the node is actually built there

deferred_beats.title: Heterotaxy — when the body cannot decide
deferred_beats.narration: Worse than a mirror image is no decision at all. In right isomerism the embryo builds two right sides: two trilobed lungs, a midline liver, no spleen, and severe cardiac defects — the asplenia or Ivemark syndrome. In left isomerism it builds two left sides: two bilobed lungs and several small spleens, with milder cardiac lesions but conduction problems. The clinical hook is the spleen. An asplenic child needs pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus cover and prophylactic penicillin, and Howell-Jolly bodies on the film are the clue that the spleen is not working.
deferred_beats.why_not_a_view: Isomerism is a WHOLE-BODY finding: two trilobed lungs, a midline liver, absent spleen. This model builds one heart and nothing else, so the scene can only assert it, never show it.
deferred_beats.belongs_in: a situs / laterality scene covering the thoracoabdominal organs, which does not exist yet

deferred_beats.title: How to answer a laterality question in three steps
deferred_beats.narration: Answer these questions in a fixed order and they stop being confusing. First, where are the atria — normal, mirrored, or ambiguous. Second, which way did the ventricles loop, D or L. Third, where do the great arteries come off. Situs, loop, connections. A child can be abnormal at any one of the three, and naming which one is abnormal is most of the diagnosis.
deferred_beats.why_not_a_view: Situs, loop, connections is a DRILL — a fixed order to answer in, not a thing to look at. It is the best revision content in this scene and it does not belong in a 3D view.
deferred_beats.belongs_in: the recall / drill layer, where a fixed-order checklist is the native form
